It does not mean the change happens automatically or by itself; a person or a system generally has to deliberately make the change happen. It does not mean unlimited or infinite change. And it does not mean the thing is fragile or unstable. Many adjustable things — like a heavy-duty adjustable wrench or a steel office chair — are extremely strong and sturdy. Adjustable simply means they have an intentional, controlled flexibility built into them.
Ease of use is often implied

Here is a subtlety worth knowing. In everyday language, when we call something "adjustable," we usually imply that the change is reasonably easy to make — that it was designed to be changed without a huge effort or special expertise. If something could technically be changed but requires a specialist, a factory, or enormous effort, we would not usually call it "adjustable" in conversation. The word carries a quiet suggestion of convenience and accessibility.
The opposite

The opposite of adjustable is fixed, rigid, or non-adjustable — meaning something set permanently in one position or form that cannot be changed. A fixed shelf in a bookcase always stays at the same height no matter what. An adjustable shelf can be moved up or down to different heights depending on what you need to store. "Fixed" = no change possible. "Adjustable" = change is possible and designed for.
Example sentences

"This desk is adjustable, so both tall and short people can use it comfortably."

"The doctor said the medication dosage is adjustable — it can be increased if needed."

"We need a more adjustable meeting time, since not everyone is free at 9 AM."

"The loan has an adjustable interest rate, which means the monthly payment amount can change over the years."

"The camera is mounted on an adjustable arm, so you can position it anywhere around the desk."
Comparing degrees

Like most adjectives, "adjustable" can be used in degrees of comparison. You can say something is more adjustable than another thing (it offers greater flexibility or more range of change) or the most adjustable option available. For example: "Of all the chairs in the store, this one is the most adjustable — you can change the height, the armrests, the backrest angle, and the seat tilt."
Related word forms

Adjust is the verb — it means to make a deliberate change: "Please adjust the mirror before you drive." Adjustment is the noun — it refers to the act of changing or the result of a change: "A small adjustment to the plan made everything work better." Non-adjustable is the adjective for the opposite condition: "The seat is non-adjustable, so it stays in one fixed position."
The one-line summary
If you ever need to recall the meaning in a flash: adjustable = designed to be changed in a controlled way, within limits, to fit different needs.
342: An adjutant is a military officer who serves as an administrative assistant and right-hand man to a senior commanding officer. Think of the adjutant as the person who keeps everything organized around the commander, so the commander can focus on leading and making decisions.
The Main Meaning: A Military Officer

In the military, every battalion, regiment, or brigade — basically any significant unit — has an adjutant. This person is not just a low-level helper; they are themselves an officer, but their job is to support a higher-ranking commanding officer.

What exactly does an adjutant do?

  • They handle all the administrative and organizational work of the unit — paperwork, records, correspondence, and official documentation.
  • They receive the commander's orders and communicate those orders formally to the rest of the unit. In older armies especially, the adjutant would read out orders aloud to assembled troops.
  • They coordinate between different sections, departments, or units on behalf of the commander.
  • They manage the daily functioning of the headquarters — schedules, rosters, personnel records, and similar matters.
  • In battle situations, they may relay the commander's instructions and ensure coordination happens smoothly.

Essentially, a commanding officer can't do everything alone. The adjutant is the person who makes sure all the administrative machinery runs properly, so nothing falls through the cracks. If the commander is the brain, the adjutant is often the hands that execute all the organizational tasks.

A simple way to picture it: Imagine the most senior general of an army base. He has strategy to think about, troops to command, and decisions to make. He cannot personally track every piece of paperwork, every official correspondence, every order that needs to be drafted and distributed. The adjutant does all of that. The adjutant is the officer right beside him, keeping the administrative world in order.

An adjutant is typically a relatively junior officer (in many armies, a captain or a lieutenant), but because of their direct access to the commander and their role in communications and records, they carry considerable importance and authority within the unit. When the adjutant speaks, people understand they are often speaking on behalf of the commander.

In many armies, there is also a higher position called the Adjutant General — a senior officer who handles personnel administration, records, and military manpower at an army-wide or national level. Think of this as the adjutant's role scaled up to an entire army or country.

While "adjutant" is almost always a military term, you will occasionally see it used more loosely to describe any close aide or administrative assistant to someone in a position of authority. However, this usage is rare, and when you encounter the word, it almost certainly refers to the military role.

There is a second, entirely different meaning of the word. An adjutant is also the common name for a large species of stork found in South Asia and Southeast Asia — specifically the Greater Adjutant and the Lesser Adjutant.

These birds got this name because of the way they walk: stiff, upright, and formal — almost like a soldier standing at attention or marching with rigid posture. People thought they looked like military adjutants on parade. They are large, somewhat ungainly birds, often seen near wetlands, garbage dumps, and open fields.

So if someone in a wildlife or nature context mentions an adjutant, they are talking about this bird, not a military officer.

SenseWhat it means
Military (primary)An officer who assists a senior commander with administration, communications, and organization
Bird (secondary)A large stork in South/Southeast Asia, named for its stiff, soldier-like posture

Think of the word "adjust" — an adjutant adjusts and manages everything around the commander, making sure the unit runs smoothly. The adjutant is the person who adjusts the system so that the leader can lead without being buried in details.
343:
If something is adjuvant, it means it is helping, assisting, or boosting something else — but crucially, it is not the main thing doing the work. It plays a supporting role that makes the primary thing more effective.

Think of it this way: if a superhero is the main fighter, an adjuvant is the sidekick who makes the superhero stronger, faster, or more effective. The sidekick doesn't win the battle alone — but without the sidekick, the superhero wouldn't be as powerful.
Where You'll Actually Encounter This Word

"Adjuvant" as an adjective is almost exclusively used in medicine and science. You will very rarely, if ever, see it in everyday conversation. But within medical writing and oncology (cancer care) especially, it is extremely common.

1. Adjuvant Therapy (Medicine & Cancer Treatment)

This is the most common use of the word.

When a patient has surgery to remove a tumor, doctors sometimes follow that surgery with adjuvant therapy — such as chemotherapy, radiation, or hormone therapy. Here, the word "adjuvant" tells you that:

  • The surgery was the primary treatment (the main attack).
  • The chemotherapy or radiation is the adjuvant treatment — it comes after, in a supporting role, to mop up any cancer cells that may have been left behind and to reduce the chances of the cancer returning.

So "adjuvant chemotherapy" doesn't mean the chemotherapy is unimportant. It means it is playing a helper role relative to the surgery that came first. It's assisting the overall treatment plan.

A practical way to remember it: adjuvant therapy = backup treatment that boosts the chances of success.

2. Adjuvant Effect (Immunology & Vaccines)

In vaccine science, a substance can have an adjuvant effect, meaning it boosts the immune response triggered by the vaccine.

Vaccines work by introducing something (like a piece of a virus) to teach your immune system to recognize and fight it. Sometimes, that alone isn't enough to create a strong immune response. So scientists add a substance that has an adjuvant effect — it essentially signals your immune system to pay more attention and respond more strongly, making the vaccine more effective.

Again, the adjuvant substance is not the vaccine itself. It is the helper that makes the vaccine work better.
The One Subtle But Important Nuance

"Adjuvant" does not just mean any kind of help. It specifically implies that:

  1. There is a primary agent or treatment doing the main job.
  2. The adjuvant thing is secondary by design — it exists to support and enhance that primary thing.
  3. The adjuvant element typically could not succeed on its own in the same role.

This is what separates "adjuvant" from simply saying "helpful." Something can be helpful while still being the main tool. But something adjuvant is, by definition, the secondary, enhancing force — never the primary one.
A Simple One-Sentence Definition to Anchor It All

Adjuvant describes something that assists or enhances the power of something else, where that something else is the primary force and the adjuvant element plays a deliberate, secondary supporting role.

Whenever you see the word adjuvant, ask yourself: "What is the main thing here, and what is this playing a supporting role to?" The answer to the second part of that question is what the adjuvant thing is boosting or helping. That framing will never fail you.
344: Administration refers to the act of managing, organizing, and running something — whether that something is an organization, a process, a substance, or even an estate. The word has several closely related meanings, and once you see the thread connecting them, they all make perfect sense.
1. The process of managing or running something

This is the most fundamental meaning. When people talk about the administration of a school, a hospital, a company, or a country, they mean the ongoing work of keeping it organized, making decisions, enforcing rules, and making sure everything functions smoothly.

It is not the work itself (like teaching or treating patients) — it is the management of that work.

"The administration of the university improved greatly after the new chancellor took charge."

"Running a large hospital requires careful administration."

Think of it this way: a ship needs sailors to do the actual sailing, but it also needs someone managing the route, the crew, the supplies, and the schedule. That management is the administration.
2. The group of people who do the managing

Because administration refers to the act of managing, it naturally came to also refer to the people who carry out that management. This is the collective group — the managers, officials, and support staff — responsible for running an organization.

"The administration has decided to extend the school year."

"If you have a complaint, contact the administration."

"She works in administration at the hospital."

When you walk into a college and see signs pointing to the "Administration Building," that building is where the people who manage the college — not the teachers, but the registrars, deans, HR staff, and so on — do their work.
3. A government in power (especially in American English)

In political contexts, particularly in the United States, administration refers to the government led by a sitting president, covering the entire team of officials who govern alongside them during their term in office. It also refers to the period of that government's rule.

"The Biden administration introduced new climate policies."

"This decision was made during the previous administration."

"She served in two different administrations."

This usage makes perfect sense: a president and their appointed officials are, essentially, the people administering (managing and running) the country during that period. The word packages both the people and the era into one term.

In other countries, similar bodies might be called a "government" or "cabinet," but in American English, administration is the standard word.
4. The act of giving, applying, or dispensing something

This meaning is slightly different in feel but follows the same logic. Administration can describe the formal, controlled act of delivering or applying something — usually a substance, a duty, or a formal procedure.

"The nurse was responsible for the administration of medication to patients."

"The judge oversaw the administration of the oath."

"The administration of justice must be fair and impartial."

"The administration of the exam was delayed due to a technical issue."

Here, administration implies care, authority, and a formal process. You don't just give someone a vaccine — you administer it. The noun captures that formality. It often appears in medical, legal, and official academic contexts.
5. The legal management of a deceased person's estate

In law, administration has a specific technical meaning: it is the process of managing and settling the financial affairs of someone who has died, especially when they left no will or when the executor named in the will is unable to act.

"The court granted letters of administration to her eldest son."

"The administration of the estate took over a year to complete."

A person appointed by a court to do this is called an administrator. They collect the deceased person's assets, pay off debts, and distribute what remains to rightful heirs — all under the supervision of the court. This is a formal legal process governed by specific laws.
The thread that ties all meanings together

All five meanings share the same underlying idea: organized, authoritative oversight and management of something. Whether it's running a company, governing a country, giving a patient their medicine, or settling a dead person's financial affairs — administration always involves someone (or a group) taking formal responsibility for handling a process correctly, systematically, and with authority.
Common phrases and collocations you'll encounter

• Business/public administration — a field of study focused on managing organizations or governments
  • Under the administration of — during the time something was managed by a particular person or group
  • Administration building / office — where the management staff of an institution is located
  • Trump/Obama/Biden administration — the government and its period during a U.S. president's term
  • Letters of administration — a legal document authorizing someone to manage a deceased person's estate
  • Administration of justice / law — the formal process of applying and enforcing legal principles
  • Drug/vaccine administration — the process of delivering medication to a patient
  • School/hospital administration — the managing body of those institutions

ContextWhat "administration" means

To sum it up plainly:

  • In everyday life → the management of an organization, or the people doing that management
  • In politics (especially U.S.) → the ruling government and the era of its rule
  • In medicine/law/formal settings → the act of formally giving or applying something
  • In legal inheritance → managing the estate of someone who has died

Master these five meanings and the word administration will never confuse you again — in a news article, a doctor's office, a legal document, or a conversation about politics.
345:
Almost every organized group — a company, a school, a government, a hospital — has two distinct layers of work happening at the same time.

The first layer is the main work: the actual purpose the organization exists for. Doctors treat patients. Teachers teach students. Engineers design bridges. This is the skilled, specialized work at the heart of everything.

The second layer is the management work: the organizing, coordinating, planning, and record-keeping that keeps the whole operation running smoothly behind the scenes. This second layer is what the word administrative describes.

So "administrative" means relating to the management and organization of something — whether that something is a company, a government, a school, or any institution.

Consider a hospital. The surgeons performing operations, and the nurses caring for patients — that is clinical (medical) work. But someone also has to schedule the appointments, maintain patient records, manage the budget, process insurance claims, and coordinate between departments. That is the administrative work. The people doing it hold administrative roles, and the office or department they work in is often called the administrative office or simply the administration.

The same logic applies anywhere. In a school, the teachers teach — but the principal, the registrar, and the office staff handle enrollment, timetables, school policies, and correspondence. That is the school's administrative side. In a business, the engineers or salespeople do the core work, while HR managers, office coordinators, and executive assistants handle the administrative operations.
Breaking down the most common uses

Administrative tasks or duties are the day-to-day management activities that keep an organization functioning — things like filing documents, scheduling meetings, processing paperwork, writing official correspondence, managing budgets, and maintaining records. They are not glamorous, but they are essential. Without them, even the most skilled doctors, teachers, or engineers would be lost in chaos.

Administrative staff (also called administrative personnel or admin staff) are the people whose specific job is to handle these management duties. Job titles like office manager, department coordinator, executive assistant, secretary, and registrar are all administrative roles.

An administrative decision is a decision made by those who manage or govern something, about how that thing is run or organized. For example, a university deciding to change its application process is an administrative decision. It is not a decision about academic content — it is a decision about running the institution. Similarly, a company deciding to reorganize its departments is an administrative decision.

An administrative error is a mistake that happened in the management or record-keeping process — not in the core work itself. If a hospital books two patients for the same appointment slot, that is an administrative error. If a surgeon makes a mistake during a procedure, that is a medical error. The distinction matters because it tells you where and how the mistake occurred.

Administrative procedures are the official, formal steps and processes that an organization requires people to follow in order to get things done. Filling out a form, submitting a request in writing, going through the right channels of approval — these are all parts of administrative procedure. They exist to keep things orderly, transparent, and consistent.

The word carries special weight when it comes to government, and this is worth understanding on its own.

Modern governments are typically divided into three branches: the legislative branch (which creates laws), the judicial branch (which interprets laws through courts), and the executive branch (which carries out and manages the laws in everyday life). The executive branch — made up of government departments, agencies, and offices — is fundamentally administrative in nature. It does not make the law; it administers it, meaning it puts the law into practice, enforces it, and manages the systems it creates.

This is why government bodies like a tax authority, an immigration department, an environmental protection agency, or a public health department are called administrative agencies. They administer — meaning they manage and carry out — the policies and rules that the law establishes.

Because these agencies wield significant power over people's lives (they can grant licenses, impose fines, deny permits, and make binding decisions), an entire branch of law called administrative law exists specifically to govern how they must behave. Administrative law sets the rules for what procedures agencies must follow, what powers they do and do not have, and how citizens can challenge or appeal their decisions. If a government agency makes a decision you disagree with — say, rejecting your visa application — you would typically pursue what is called an administrative appeal, which is a formal challenge within the administrative system before turning to the courts.
The feeling and tone of the word

In most everyday uses, "administrative" is a neutral, professional word. It simply describes the management and organizational side of things.

However, it sometimes takes on a slightly heavy or frustrated tone, especially in phrases like administrative burden, administrative overhead, or administrative red tape. These phrases acknowledge that management processes — while necessary — can pile up into exhausting quantities of paperwork, approval chains, and procedures that slow things down. "Administrative red tape" in particular refers to bureaucratic rules and processes that feel excessive or needlessly complicated.

On the positive side, phrases like administrative support, administrative leadership, and administrative excellence show the word being used with respect and appreciation — recognizing that good, efficient management is genuinely valuable.

"Administrative" describes anything that relates to managing, organizing, governing, or coordinating the operations of an institution, organization, or system — rather than the core, specialized work that the organization exists to perform. When something is called administrative, it belongs to the world of planning, record-keeping, decision-making about how things are run, and the formal procedures that keep organized groups functioning.
346:
"Admirable" describes someone or something that genuinely deserves respect, deep approval, and a feeling of looking up to it. When you call something admirable, you are saying it has a quality or has done something so good, so worthy, or so excellent that it naturally earns honest respect from the people who see it.

Think of it this way: when you witness something that makes you think, "Wow — that is truly worthy of respect," the thing you are looking at is admirable.
The Feeling Behind the Word

The word "admirable" is rooted in the idea of admiration — a sincere, warm feeling that combines respect with a kind of wonder. This is important because "admirable" is stronger than simply calling something "good" or "nice." You can like a meal. You can enjoy a song. But admiration — and therefore the label "admirable" — involves a deeper recognition: this thing rises above the ordinary and genuinely deserves to be looked up to.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Admirable?

Almost anything can be admirable — a person, a character trait, a decision, an action, or an achievement. But it is most naturally used for:

Moral qualities — like courage, honesty, patience, integrity, kindness, or dedication. These are the kinds of virtues that earn admiration because they are hard to maintain and represent the best of human character. "Her admirable patience never faltered, even in the most difficult moments."

Behavior in tough situations — when someone handles hardship, pressure, or challenge with grace. "He showed admirable composure during the crisis."

Achievements — things accomplished through great skill, effort, or persistence. "Her admirable performance in the competition left everyone speechless."

Ideas, plans, or solutions — when something is so well thought-out that it earns genuine intellectual respect. "That is an admirable approach to a very complicated problem."
How Strong Is the Word?

"Admirable" is a fairly strong word — not something you throw around casually. You would not describe a pleasant afternoon or a decent cup of coffee as "admirable." It is reserved for things that genuinely stand out, that go above the ordinary level, and that earn honest, deep respect.

That said, it is not the absolute peak of praise either. It sits in the range of sincere, solid, dignified approval — not breathless excitement, but real, thoughtful esteem.
A Subtle Shade: Admirable Can Imply Mild Surprise

Sometimes, "admirable" carries a quiet sense of pleasant surprise — as if the speaker did not fully expect such a high quality and is genuinely impressed by it. For example: "For someone so new to the job, her leadership skills are quite admirable." This doesn't mean she is barely good enough — it means she is impressively good, and the speaker is noting how that quality stands out even more given the context.
Synonyms — and How They Differ

Knowing the differences between similar words sharpens your understanding of "admirable."

Praiseworthy is very close, but leans more toward being worthy of verbal praise specifically. "Admirable" carries a slightly deeper emotional weight — it's about inner respect and wonder, not just saying something nice.

Commendable means worthy of positive recognition. It's a bit more formal and institutional — you might find it in official reports or evaluations. "Admirable" feels more personal and heartfelt.

Laudable is a formal, literary synonym meaning highly worthy of praise. It means the same thing as "admirable" in most cases, but it is rarely used in everyday conversation.

Exemplary means so good that it can serve as a model or example for others to follow. It's slightly stronger than "admirable" and carries the added meaning of being a standard worth copying.

Remarkable means surprisingly unusual or impressive — but it lacks the moral or virtuous weight that "admirable" often carries. A strange coincidence can be remarkable, but not admirable. Admirable almost always implies that something good about character, effort, or virtue is being recognized.

Impressive focuses on the reaction — being struck by something great — but again, without the sense of moral worthiness that "admirable" carries.
Antonyms — The Opposites

The opposites of admirable are words like disgraceful (deserving shame), deplorable (extremely bad and worthy of strong condemnation), contemptible (deserving scorn), and shameful (causing or deserving shame). These give you a clear picture of the territory "admirable" occupies at the positive end of the spectrum.
Words That Naturally Go With "Admirable"

In real usage, you will most often see "admirable" paired with words like: admirable courage, admirable patience, admirable dedication, admirable restraint, admirable honesty, admirable composure, admirable qualities. As intensifiers, people say truly admirable, genuinely admirable, or thoroughly admirable.
Tone and Register

"Admirable" is slightly formal in tone. You will encounter it more in writing, speeches, journalism, and careful conversation than in casual everyday chatter. In very informal speech, people might say "awesome," "incredible," or "really impressive" instead. But "admirable" carries more gravity and dignity than those words — it signals thoughtful, earned respect rather than an excited reaction.
Example Sentences

Here are sentences that show the word in action, from simple to more nuanced:

"She showed admirable courage when she stood up for what was right."

"His dedication to helping others is truly admirable."

"What you did was admirable — very few people would have made the same sacrifice."

"The team displayed admirable discipline throughout the entire competition."

"While I disagree with his methods, his commitment to fairness is admirable."

That last sentence is particularly revealing. Notice that "admirable" can be used to recognize one specific quality in someone, even when you disapprove of other aspects of who they are. This shows the word's precision — it targets a quality, not necessarily a whole person.
The Single-Line Summary

Admirable means genuinely deserving of deep respect and sincere approval — because a quality, action, or achievement rises above the ordinary and naturally earns the honest admiration of those who witness it.
347:
Admiration is a warm, pleasant feeling you get when you see or think about someone or something that you find genuinely impressive, excellent, or worthy of praise. It combines respect and approval with a positive emotional warmth — not just a cold, calculated judgment, but a feeling that carries a kind of glow with it.

When you feel admiration, you are recognizing that something or someone has a quality — a skill, a character trait, an achievement, or a beauty — that stands clearly above the ordinary. You look at it and think: "This is remarkable. This deserves to be acknowledged."

Admiration can be directed at many different kinds of things:

People — for their courage, talent, intelligence, kindness, hard work, achievements, or moral character. You might admire a scientist who has spent her life finding cures for diseases, or a friend who stayed calm and helped others during a crisis.

Objects and places — the beauty of a painting, a building, a mountain landscape, or a piece of music. When you stand before the Taj Mahal and feel a sense of wonder at its beauty and craftsmanship, that feeling is admiration.

Qualities and actions — a selfless act, an honest decision made at great personal cost, extraordinary dedication, or brilliant creativity. Importantly, you don't have to admire a whole person — you can admire a specific quality they have or a specific thing they did.

Admiration is not just intellectual recognition. It carries genuine warmth. When you admire someone, you feel good just thinking about them. There is often a desire to appreciate them, to pay attention to them, to learn from them, or simply to acknowledge what they have done or who they are.

It can feel like a quiet sense of pleasure — the kind you feel when you watch a master musician play, read a beautifully written sentence, or witness an act of extraordinary human kindness.

Admiration exists on a scale from mild to very deep:

Mild admiration: "I noticed that she handled that difficult situation very gracefully. I admire that about her." — It is quiet and perhaps passing, but it is real.

Deep, lasting admiration: Someone who has inspired you for years — whose courage, wisdom, or genius has genuinely shaped the way you think about life. This kind of admiration is sustained, heartfelt, and sometimes life-changing.
How admiration differs from similar feelings

This is one of the most useful things to understand, because admiration is often confused with nearby emotions.

Admiration vs. envy: Envy is when you want what someone else has and feel resentful or unhappy because you do not have it. Admiration is when you genuinely appreciate what someone has, without bitterness and without necessarily wanting it for yourself. You can admire a great dancer without wishing you were a dancer. Envy shrinks you; admiration does not.

Admiration vs. respect: Respect is closely related to admiration but tends to be cooler and more formal. You respect someone when you recognize their authority, competence, or rights. Admiration includes that recognition but adds emotional warmth and a sense of being genuinely moved or impressed. You might respect a strict but fair employer, while you admire a mentor who lights a fire in you.

Admiration vs. love: Love is deep personal attachment — it is about a relationship. Admiration does not require personal closeness. You can admire a historical figure you have never met and never will. You can admire someone without loving them, and you can love someone without fully admiring them (though the two often go together beautifully).

Admiration vs. awe: Awe is what you feel when something is so grand or overwhelming that it makes you feel very small — like standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon or watching a violent thunderstorm over the ocean. Awe can be part of admiration, but admiration is warmer and more personal. Awe sometimes carries an edge of fear or smallness; admiration is purely positive.

Admiration vs. idolization: Idolization is an excessive, uncritical, and somewhat blind form of admiration — when you admire someone so intensely that you see no flaws in them, placing them on an unreachable pedestal. Healthy admiration can acknowledge that someone is imperfect while still genuinely valuing their excellent qualities. Idolization cannot.

Admiration is typically earned rather than given automatically. Things that commonly earn it:

  • Excellence — reaching a very high level in something: athletic greatness, intellectual mastery, artistic skill.
  • Virtue — showing qualities like honesty, courage, generosity, and integrity — especially when doing so is difficult or costly.
  • Persistence — working hard and never giving up, especially in the face of great obstacles or repeated failure.
  • Originality — thinking in a way no one has thought before, or creating something truly new and meaningful.
  • Selflessness — putting others before yourself, sacrificing your own comfort or advantage for someone else's benefit.

Admiration is not always spoken aloud. It can be expressed in several ways:

Verbally — telling someone directly, or telling others: "I really admire how she handled that," or "He is one of the most admirable people I've ever met."

By close attention — watching someone perform, reading everything they have written, or following their work carefully over time. Paying close, willing attention is itself a quiet form of admiration.

By imitation — trying to adopt the qualities or approach of the person you admire. If you admire someone's patience, you try to be more patient yourself. This is arguably the most meaningful form of admiration — it improves you.

By praise — publicly acknowledging someone's achievements or qualities, making sure others see what you see.

"hold someone in admiration" — to think of someone with a lasting, respectful admiration.
"I have always held her in great admiration."

"earn someone's admiration" — to do something that causes someone to admire you.
"His bravery during the rescue earned the admiration of the entire community."

"worthy of admiration" — deserving to be admired.
"Her dedication to her work is truly worthy of admiration."

"mutual admiration" — when two people admire each other.
"There was a clear mutual admiration between the two scientists."

"admiration for" — the most natural preposition used with this noun.
"She expressed her admiration for the artist's work."

"lost in admiration" — so deeply moved by admiration that you are momentarily still or speechless.
"He stood lost in admiration before the ancient sculpture."

1. "The crowd watched in silent admiration as the gymnast completed her routine without a single error."
  2. "Her admiration for her grandmother's quiet strength only grew as she learned more about what the woman had endured."
  3. "He had always felt a deep admiration for teachers who could make complicated things simple."
  4. "The novel received widespread admiration for its honesty and the beauty of its language."
  5. "It takes nothing away from your own abilities to feel admiration for someone else's talent."
  6. "His colleagues spoke of him with great admiration, praising both his skill and his personal decency."
  7. "She looked at the mountains with the kind of admiration that made her feel, for a moment, very peaceful."

Admiration is a generous emotion. It costs you nothing to feel it, and it does not diminish you in any way. When you genuinely admire someone, it reflects well on you — it shows that you are capable of recognizing greatness and goodness outside yourself.

It is also one of the emotions that can quietly guide and shape you. The things you find yourself admiring most often reveal a great deal about what you value and, perhaps, what you quietly hope to become.
348:
To admire someone or something means to look at them or think about them with a feeling of genuine pleasure, respect, and appreciation — because you find them impressive, excellent, or beautiful in some way.

When you admire something, you are not just noticing it. You are moved by it. There is an inner sense of "this is remarkable" or "this is truly good."
What the Feeling Actually Is

Admiration is a blend of three things happening at once:

  • Pleasure — it feels good to see or think about what you admire
  • Respect — you hold it in high regard; you recognize its worth
  • Being impressed — you feel that what you're looking at is above ordinary, better than average, or genuinely special

All three usually come together. If you only feel pleasure but not respect, that is more like enjoying something. If you only feel respect but no pleasure or impression, that is closer to simply tolerating something. Admiration is when all three combine.
What Can You Admire?

You can admire a very wide range of things:

People — for their character, their achievements, their skills, or how they handle life. "I admire my grandmother for her patience and kindness."

Qualities in people — even without admiring the whole person, you can admire a specific trait. "I admire his honesty, even when it cost him."

Achievements and work — great pieces of art, music, writing, architecture, scientific discoveries. "She stood in the museum and admired the painting for a long time."

Nature and beauty — a mountain view, a sunset, an elegant building, a perfectly made object. "They stopped at the edge of the cliff to admire the valley below."

Abstract things — a person's courage in a difficult situation, a company's dedication to quality, a team's discipline. "I admire the way they handled the crisis."
A Key Feature: Admiration Looks Upward

This is important. When you admire something, there is almost always a sense that what you are admiring is above you in some way — more skilled, more beautiful, more virtuous, or more impressive than the ordinary. You are looking up at it, even if only slightly.

This is why we say things like "I look up to her" as a natural way to express admiration. The direction — upward — is built into the feeling.

You do not need to be inferior to admire something. A great musician can admire another great musician. But the act of admiring always involves recognizing something as worthy of that high regard.
You Do Not Need to Know Them

You can admire a person you have never met — a historical figure, a famous scientist, an athlete you have only seen on screen. "He admired Einstein deeply, even though Einstein had died before he was born."

Admiration does not require a personal relationship. It only requires that you have come to know enough about the person or thing to feel that deep sense of respect and impression.
Degrees: How Strongly Can You Admire?

Admiration can range from mild to very deep:

  • Mild: "I admire the way they designed this product." (You are impressed, but it's not a life-changing feeling.)
  • Moderate: "I admire her dedication to her work." (Clear, genuine respect and appreciation.)
  • Deep: "I deeply admire the courage it took to do that." / "I have always greatly admired his writing." (Strong, sincere, lasting admiration.)

Words like deeply, truly, greatly, sincerely, and genuinely are commonly used to show that the admiration is strong and real.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding admire becomes sharper when you see how it sits among related words:

Like — You like things that simply please you or that you enjoy. It's ordinary and comfortable. Admiration goes further: it involves being impressed. You can like a casual song on the radio, but you admire a musician's extraordinary talent.

Love — Love is a much deeper emotional bond, often personal and intimate. You can admire someone greatly without loving them. And you can love someone (like a family member) without necessarily admiring them.

Respect — This overlaps the most with admire. But respect is more about recognizing someone's rights, position, or authority — it can be given even to someone you don't find impressive. Admiration always includes a sense of being genuinely moved or impressed. You might respect a difficult boss without admiring them. But if you admire someone, respect is almost always part of it too.

Idolize — This is admiration taken to an extreme. To idolize someone is to admire them so much that you put them on a pedestal and refuse to see their flaws. Admiration is healthy and grounded. Idolization is excessive and often blind.

Envy — Envy is wanting what someone else has, often with a sting of resentment. Admiration is appreciating what someone has without necessarily wanting it for yourself, and without resentment. However, in real life, admiration and envy sometimes coexist — you can admire a person's talent while also wishing you had it. But admiration by itself has no resentment in it.
"Admire For" — The Most Natural Construction

The most common way to use the word is admire [someone] for [reason]:

  • "I admire her for never giving up."
  • "We admire the team for their discipline and focus."
  • "He is widely admired for his generosity."

This structure makes clear both who or what is being admired and why — which is the complete picture of admiration.
Grudging Admiration

Sometimes you admire someone even though you do not want to — perhaps because they are your rival, or because they did something you disagree with, but you cannot deny the skill or quality involved. This is called grudging admiration: "I have to admit a grudging admiration for the way they handled that situation, even though they are our competitors."

This shows that admiration is honest and sometimes involuntary. The feeling arises when something is genuinely impressive, even if the circumstances are uncomfortable.
Sarcastic Use (Rare)

In everyday speech, people sometimes use "admire" sarcastically to mean the opposite — "I admire your confidence" said to someone who just made an embarrassing mistake, meaning "Your nerve surprises me." This is an ironic use. The real meaning of the word remains positive; context tells you when it is being used this way.
Summary in One Line
To admire is to feel genuine pleasure, respect, and a sense of being impressed by someone or something — recognizing it as truly excellent, beautiful, or worthy in some way.
349:
An admirer is a person who looks at someone — or occasionally something — and feels a deep, genuine sense of appreciation, respect, and wonder. The admirer sees a quality, talent, achievement, or trait and is genuinely moved by it. They don't just notice it; they hold it in high regard.

Think of it this way: when you see a skilled musician perform and feel a strong, warm sense of "that person is truly remarkable," you become their admirer.
The two main ways the word is used

1. General admiration (respect, appreciation)

Here, an admirer is someone who deeply respects and appreciates another person's talent, character, work, or achievements. This has nothing to do with romance — it is pure, sincere appreciation.

  • "He is a great admirer of Dr. APJ Abdul Kalam."
    (He deeply respects and looks up to Kalam's life and work.)
  • "Her paintings have admirers all over the world."
    (Many people across the world genuinely appreciate and value her art.)
  • "As a young scientist, she was an admirer of Marie Curie."
    (She held Curie in high regard and was inspired by her.)

2. Romantic admiration

This is the other very common use of the word. Here, an admirer is someone who is attracted to another person, holds them in high regard, and has warm, affectionate feelings toward them — but may not have expressed those feelings yet, or may not be in a relationship with that person.

This use carries a slightly old-fashioned, gentle, and respectful quality. An admirer in this sense is not just someone who finds another person physically attractive; the word implies genuine feeling and a sense that the other person is special.

  • "She received a bouquet of roses from a secret admirer."
    (Someone who has feelings for her but hasn't revealed their identity.)
  • "He had been her admirer for years before he finally gathered the courage to speak to her."
    (He quietly held affectionate, appreciative feelings for her over a long time.)
  • "She had no shortage of admirers, but she wasn't interested in any of them."
    (Many people were romantically drawn to her and admired her.)
What exactly makes someone an "admirer" — and not just someone who "likes"?

The key difference is depth and sincerity.

If you casually like something, you're not necessarily an admirer. An admirer feels something stronger — a genuine sense that the person being admired has exceptional, notable, or impressive qualities. The feeling has weight to it. It involves appreciation, respect, and often a kind of quiet wonder.

An admirer is moved by what they see. They think about it. They speak of it with warmth. They feel that the person they admire is truly worthy of that admiration.
The tone and feel of the word

The word "admirer" has a warm, dignified, and positive tone. It never carries a negative meaning on its own.

When used in a romantic context, it has a somewhat classic, old-world quality to it — it implies that the person admiring is doing so with respect and care, not just desire. This is why it often appears in literature and formal writing. It's a gentler, more refined way of saying someone has feelings for another person.

When used in a general context, it signals that the appreciation is genuine and personal — not just vague or casual.

This is one of the most commonly used phrases with the word. A secret admirer is someone who has warm or romantic feelings for another person but keeps those feelings hidden — the person being admired does not know who is feeling this way. The phrase is widely used in everyday life, stories, films, and greeting cards.

Fan — A fan is also someone who admires, usually a celebrity, athlete, or public figure. But "fan" feels more enthusiastic and group-like (fans of a cricket team, fans of a singer). An "admirer" feels more personal, individual, and thoughtful.

Supporter — A supporter backs someone's work or cause. An admirer goes deeper — they feel genuine personal appreciation, not just agreement or backing.

Suitor — In a romantic context, a suitor is someone who is actively and openly pursuing a relationship. An admirer may simply feel the appreciation quietly, without necessarily pursuing anything.

Enthusiast — An enthusiast is passionate about a subject or activity (a music enthusiast, a cricket enthusiast). An admirer is focused specifically on a person.
Can "admirer" describe admiration of things, not people?

Yes, though this is less common. It works perfectly well:

  • "He is a lifelong admirer of classical Indian architecture."

However, most naturally, the word is used for admiring people — their talent, character, achievements, or personality.

An admirer is a person who holds deep, genuine appreciation and respect for someone (or occasionally something). In everyday life, the word is used in two main ways: to describe someone who deeply respects another person's talent or character, and to describe someone who has warm romantic feelings for another person. In both cases, the feeling is sincere, personal, and carries real weight — it is never casual or superficial. The word itself carries a warm, dignified, and positive tone.
350: Before diving into the different meanings, it helps to know the one thread running through all of them: letting something (or someone) in. "Admit" always involves allowing access — whether that's a person into a building, a student into a school, or a truth out into the open. Keep this image in mind and the meanings will all feel logical.
Meaning 1 — To confess or acknowledge something, especially something uncomfortable

This is the most common everyday use. When you "admit" something, you are saying out loud a truth that you were holding back, resisting, or perhaps even hiding — and now you are finally releasing it.

"He admitted that he had eaten the last piece of food."
"She admitted her mistake."
"I admit I was wrong."

The key feeling here is reluctance before honesty. "Admit" always carries a quiet suggestion that the truth didn't come easily — that there was some resistance, some delay, some discomfort. This is what makes it different from just "say." If you simply say "I was wrong," you're stating a fact. If you admit you were wrong, you're implying it took some effort to get there.

This is also why "admit" works so well in serious or formal contexts. A suspect "admits" guilt. A leader "admits" failure. A person "admits" they don't know the answer. In each case, there's something at stake, and the truth is being surrendered rather than volunteered freely.

Grammatically, you can use "admit" in a few different patterns here:

After "admit," you can put a that-clause: "He admitted that he was scared." You can also put a noun directly: "She admitted the truth." Or you can use "to" followed by a noun or a gerund (a verb ending in -ing): "He admitted to the theft." / "She admitted to lying."

"Admit that" and "admit to" are both correct, but they feel slightly different. "I admit that I lied" is direct and clear. "I admit to lying" sounds slightly more formal, like something you'd hear in a courtroom or an official setting.

How is "admit" different from similar words?

Confess is stronger and more serious. You confess to a crime, a sin, or a deep wrongdoing. "Admit" works for everything — from "I admit I forgot to call" to "I admit I broke the law." The smaller the thing, the more natural "admit" sounds. The heavier and more morally loaded the thing, the more natural "confess" sounds.

Acknowledge is cooler and more neutral. If you acknowledge something, you are simply recognizing it as true — without the emotional weight of reluctance. "She acknowledged that the report had errors" sounds professional and calm. "She admitted that the report had errors" suggests it was harder to say, perhaps because she was responsible for those errors.
Meaning 2 — To allow someone to enter a place

Here, "admit" means to physically permit entry — to let someone in.

"This ticket admits two people."
"Children under 12 are not admitted."
"The security guard admitted them into the building."

When "admit" is used this way, it implies a deliberate, often official decision to grant access. This is why "admit" sounds more formal than "let in." A bouncer lets someone in. A hospital admits a patient. There's a process, a gatekeeping, a considered decision.

The most important example of this use in everyday English is being admitted to a hospital. This doesn't just mean walking into a hospital — it specifically means you were formally received as an inpatient (someone who will stay there for treatment), as opposed to a visitor or an outpatient who comes and goes. So "She was admitted to the hospital" is a specific, medical use you will encounter often.

Similarly, "admit" is used in legal settings: "The judge admitted the new evidence into the trial." This means the judge allowed the evidence to be officially used in court. The same gatekeeping logic applies.
Meaning 3 — To formally accept someone into a school, organization, or profession

This meaning is closely related to Meaning 2, but instead of physical entry, it's about long-term membership or formal acceptance into a group after meeting certain conditions.

"She was admitted to Harvard University." (The university accepted her as a student.)
"He was admitted to the bar." (He became a licensed lawyer after meeting the requirements.)
"The organization only admits members who pass the screening process."

Universities, professional bodies, clubs, and associations all "admit" people. The word signals that there was a process, a set of standards, and a formal decision — and the person was found worthy of entry. It is never casual.
Meaning 4 (Formal) — "Admit of" — to allow for the possibility of something

This is a more literary and formal use that you will mostly encounter in written English, especially in older texts, formal writing, legal language, or philosophy. The key phrase is "admit of," and it means to allow for or to make room for a possibility.

"This rule admits of no exceptions." (The rule allows no exceptions whatsoever.)
"The problem admits of only one solution." (There is only one possible answer to this problem.)
"His behavior admits of no excuse." (His behavior cannot be excused in any way.)

Think of it as the rule or situation acting like a door — it is either letting certain possibilities in, or keeping them out. "Admits of no exceptions" means the rule is a locked door: nothing gets through. This usage is declining in everyday modern speech but it is still alive in formal and academic writing, so it's worth knowing.
A Subtle but Important Note: Why "Admit" and Not Just "Let In"?

You might wonder why English uses "admit" when simpler phrases like "let in" or "accept" could work. The answer is that "admit" carries a sense of formality, process, and deliberate decision-making. A parent lets a child into the house. A hospital admits a patient. A university admits a student. A court admits evidence. Wherever there is an institution, a formal procedure, an official judgment — "admit" is the natural choice.

Confessing or acknowledging: "She admitted she had made a mistake."
Physical entry: "The ticket admits one adult."
Formal acceptance into an institution: "He was admitted to the law school."
Allowing a possibility (formal): "This contract admits of no ambiguity."
Common conversational phrase: "I have to admit, that surprised me." / "I'll admit, I didn't expect that."

That last set — "I have to admit" and "I'll admit" — are very natural, casual ways to introduce a confession of something surprising, unexpected, or slightly uncomfortable. You will hear these constantly in everyday speech.
351:
Imagine you are making tea. You start with hot water, drop in a teabag, and then add a small spoonful of honey. That honey — the thing you are adding into the main substance — is an admixture. It's something that is mixed into something else.

An admixture is a thing that is added to another substance to form a mixture, or it is the resulting mixture itself. The word captures both ideas: the ingredient being mixed in, and the blended result of that mixing.
The Two Senses of the Word

Admixture has two closely related meanings that you should know:

First, it can mean the thing that is added — the ingredient, the element, the substance being mixed in. In this sense, it's the "add-in," not the main thing. If you dissolve a pinch of salt into a glass of water, the salt is the admixture. The water is the primary substance; the salt is what gets mixed into it.

Second, it can mean the result of mixing — the final blend or combination itself. In this sense, the glass of salt water, taken as a whole, is the admixture. You are calling the entire mixture by this name.

In practice, both meanings appear in real writing, and context will almost always make it clear which sense is intended. You won't get confused by this once you understand the underlying idea: admixture is about something being mixed into something else, whether you are focusing on the thing being added or on what comes out of the mixing.

In everyday and scientific language, admixture is used when one substance is physically blended into another. The key thing to notice is that an admixture does not chemically bond or permanently fuse with the main substance — the things mixed together keep their separate identities at some level, even though they are now combined.

Think of sand mixed into cement, or a dye stirred into paint. Nothing new is being created chemically; things are just being blended together. That blended element, or the result of the blending, is an admixture.

In the world of construction and concrete, this word has a very specific and well-known use. Builders add special substances to concrete — chemicals or materials that change how the concrete behaves — to make it dry faster, flow more easily, resist water, or become stronger. These added substances are officially called admixtures in the construction industry. When an engineer says "we used an admixture in this concrete pour," they mean a deliberate, controlled additive was blended in for a specific purpose.

Admixture is also used in a powerful figurative sense — to describe abstract qualities, emotions, or ideas that are blended together in something.

For example:

  • A politician's speech might be described as delivered with an admixture of passion and cold calculation — meaning both qualities were present at once, woven together.
  • A novel might be said to have an admixture of comedy and grief — sadness and humor are mixed into the texture of the story.
  • A person's personality might contain an admixture of generosity and pride.

In all these cases, the word is doing the same job: pointing to something that is blended into a larger whole. The things being mixed are not physical materials here, but they are still being "combined" in the way you experience them. Figurative use is common in literature, criticism, and thoughtful writing.

This is one of the most important and widely used technical applications of the word today. In genetics, admixture refers to the mixing of genetic material between two or more populations that were previously separate from each other.

When two groups of humans (or animals or plants) that evolved apart from one another come into contact and produce offspring together, the descendants carry genes from both ancestral groups. Scientists say those descendants show admixture. It is the genetic trace of populations blending over time.

For example, researchers studying ancient human history might say: "The skeletal remains showed significant admixture between early farmers and hunter-gatherer populations." This means the person's DNA carried genetic contributions from two distinct ancestral groups that had merged. The word is used neutrally and scientifically — it carries no judgment, just a description of genetic blending.
How It Differs From Similar Words

You might wonder: isn't this just the same as mixture, blend, or combination? The difference is real but subtle.

A mixture is very general — it simply means things put together. There is no sense of proportion, of one thing being the "main" substance and another being the "add-in."

A blend suggests things being smoothed together into something harmonious or uniform, often losing their separate identities in the result.

A combination is even more neutral — it just means things joined or paired.

Admixture, by contrast, carries a slightly more specific implication: there is usually a primary substance, and something is being mixed into it. It's not a 50-50 equal partnership — one thing is the base, and the admixture is what goes in. Additionally, the things mixed still retain some sense of their own identity rather than fusing into something entirely new. The word also has a more formal, precise, and technical weight to it compared to the others.
Tone and Register: When Is This Word Used?

Admixture is a formal word. You will not hear it often in casual everyday conversation — people are more likely to say "a mixture of" or "a bit of both." But you will encounter it frequently in:

  • Scientific writing (genetics, geology, chemistry, materials science)
  • Academic writing (history, sociology, anthropology)
  • Literary criticism and high-quality prose (where a writer wants to describe a subtle blending of qualities)
  • Construction and engineering (where it has a precise technical definition)

When you see it, it signals careful, precise writing. It is a word chosen deliberately, usually because the writer wants to convey the specific idea of something being mixed into something else, rather than just a general combination.

Admixture is a noun meaning:

The thing added into a primary substance to create a mix — or the mixture that results from that blending. The key ideas baked into the word are: something is going into something else, the things mixed retain some individual identity, and the focus is on controlled or deliberate blending rather than a random jumble. It works both literally (physical substances) and figuratively (abstract qualities), and it carries a formal, precise tone that makes it especially at home in scientific, academic, and literary contexts.
352:
To admonish someone means to firmly but calmly tell them that they have done something wrong, or to warn them not to do something wrong. Think of it as a serious, caring correction — not a screaming rage, but not a gentle whisper either. It sits right in the middle: firm, clear, and deliberate.

Imagine a teacher noticing a student cheating on a test. She doesn't scream at him. She doesn't ignore it either. She walks over, looks him in the eye, and says quietly but firmly: "This is unacceptable. Don't do this again." That is admonishing. The student feels the weight of her words. They sting — not because she was cruel, but because she was serious.

The word does two jobs, and both are closely related:

1. To correct someone for something they've already done wrong. This is the most common use. You admonish someone after they've made a mistake or behaved badly. The correction is pointed and firm, but it isn't a full-blown punishment — it's more of a strong verbal warning.

Example: The coach admonished his players for arriving late to practice.

2. To warn or urge someone not to do something (often before they do it). Here, you're not correcting a past mistake — you're cautioning someone about what lies ahead.

Example: She admonished him to stay away from dangerous parts of the city.

In both cases, the spirit is the same: someone who cares (or has authority) is telling another person — seriously and directly — that a certain behavior is wrong or risky.
The tone and feel of the word:

This is what makes "admonish" special and different from similar words. It carries a very specific emotional temperature:

It is not angry. You don't admonish someone in a fit of rage. If you're red in the face and shouting, that's scolding or berating, not admonishing.

It is not casual. If you lightly say "hey, maybe don't do that," that's just suggesting. Admonishing carries real weight and seriousness.

It is not purely punishing. A judge who sentences someone to prison is punishing, not admonishing. When a judge admonishes a defendant, they are delivering a firm verbal warning — words meant to sink in and change behavior.

It often comes from a place of authority or genuine concern. Parents admonish children. Mentors admonish students. Elders admonish the young. A close friend can admonish you too — but only when the situation is serious enough that they feel they must say something. The person doing the admonishing usually has some moral standing, experience, or authority that gives their words weight.

In short: admonishing is controlled, purposeful, and serious. The goal is always to correct or prevent — not to destroy, not to vent emotion.
How it differs from similar words:

Scold — Scolding is more emotional and often louder. A scolding can feel like an attack. Admonishing is calmer and more measured.

Rebuke — A rebuke is sharper and more cutting than admonishing. Rebuking is like a slap; admonishing is like a firm hand on the shoulder.

Warn — Warning focuses purely on future danger ("Watch out, that stove is hot"). Admonishing can also address past behavior and carries a moral or behavioral element.

Reprimand — A reprimand is more formal and official (like in a workplace or legal setting). Admonishing can be formal or informal.

Advise — Advising is neutral and helpful. Admonishing always has an element of correction or disapproval baked in.
More example sentences to cement it:

• The professor admonished the class for their lack of preparation.
  • His father admonished him sternly, telling him that lying was never acceptable.
  • The doctor admonished her patient to stop smoking before it was too late.
  • The judge admonished the witness to answer only what was asked.
  • She felt embarrassed when her boss admonished her in front of the team.
  • The old man admonished the teenagers to show more respect to their elders.
One-line summary you can always return to:

To admonish is to tell someone — firmly, seriously, and with genuine purpose — that their behavior is wrong or that they are heading in a dangerous direction. It is correction with weight, not cruelty.
353:
An admonishment is a firm, serious verbal warning or correction directed at someone because their behavior is wrong, inappropriate, or likely to cause problems. The person giving it disapproves of what the other person did (or is doing), and they're telling them — clearly and seriously — to stop it or do better.

It's not a punishment. It's words. The goal is to correct the person, not to hurt them.
Who gives it, and who receives it?

An admonishment almost always comes from someone who has authority, experience, or moral standing — a parent, a teacher, a boss, a judge, an elder, a mentor. They feel it's their place to speak up, and they do.

The person receiving it has done something that the giver considers wrong, careless, or beneath their standards.
The tone: firm, but not necessarily cruel

This is an important nuance. An admonishment can range from gently firm to sternly serious, but it's always deliberate and composed — not wild or emotional. The person giving it is in control of themselves. They're not screaming or losing their temper. They are telling you clearly that what you did is not acceptable, and they expect better.

Think of a quiet but serious look from a parent, followed by firm words. That's closer to an admonishment than a loud explosion of anger.

Usually one of these situations:

  • Someone behaved wrongly or irresponsibly (and is being corrected after the fact)
  • Someone is about to make a mistake or act badly (and is being warned before it happens)
  • Someone keeps repeating a bad habit and the giver has had enough of ignoring it
How it differs from similar words

These words are related but not the same:

Warning — A warning is mostly about danger ("Watch out, that road is slippery"). An admonishment is about behavior and carries moral disapproval. You can be admonished for lying; you're warned about ice on the road.

Scolding — A scolding is more emotional and heated. The person scolding you might be raising their voice or showing raw frustration. An admonishment is more composed and dignified. A grandmother who quietly sits you down and says, "That behavior is unacceptable, and I expect better from you," is giving you an admonishment. If she shouts at you for five minutes, that's more of a scolding.

Reprimand — Very close in meaning. A reprimand tends to be more official and formal — something a manager puts in your file, or a judge delivers in a courtroom. An admonishment can be personal, quiet, and private.

Lecture — A lecture is long, preachy, and often one-directional. An admonishment is pointed and concise. Your father lecturing you for an hour about responsibility is a lecture; his stopping you at the door with two firm sentences about your attitude is an admonishment.

Criticism — Criticism is about evaluating quality ("Your work was sloppy"). An admonishment is specifically about behavior and almost always carries a moral or ethical dimension ("What you did was wrong, and it must not happen again").

You'll also come across the word admonition — it means exactly the same thing. Both are noun forms of the verb admonish. "Admonition" is slightly more common in formal, literary, or religious writing. "Admonishment" is equally correct and very widely used. You can use either one without any difference in meaning.

• The judge delivered a sharp admonishment to the lawyer for interrupting the proceedings.
  • Her mother's gentle admonishment was enough to make her reconsider her words.
  • Despite repeated admonishments from his coach, he kept arriving late to practice.
  • The soldier received a formal admonishment for failing to follow protocol.
  • He took the admonishment seriously and changed his ways.
When would you naturally use this word?

Use admonishment when you want to describe a serious, firm, spoken (or written) correction about someone's behavior — especially when it comes from a position of authority or moral responsibility, and when the intent is correction rather than punishment.

It's a slightly formal word. In casual speech, people often say "he got told off," "she gave him a warning," or "they scolded him." In writing — whether formal, professional, or literary — admonishment fits naturally and precisely.

An admonishment is a serious, firm, verbal correction or warning from someone with authority or moral standing, directed at a person whose behavior is wrong, with the aim of making them stop and do better.
354:
An admonition is a serious, earnest warning or piece of cautionary advice given to someone — usually to stop them from making a mistake, to correct their behavior, or to urge them to be more careful.

Think of it as a firm, meaningful word of caution from someone who genuinely wants you to do better or stay out of trouble.

Imagine three things happening at once when an admonition is given:

  1. Someone sees a problem — a bad habit, a risky choice, a moral failing, or a rule being broken.
  2. They speak up about it — seriously, not casually.
  3. Their goal is correction or prevention — not punishment, but a genuine push toward better behavior.

That serious, caring, corrective warning? That's the admonition.
The Tone: Where It Sits on the Scale

This is important. An admonition is not a casual suggestion, and it's not a harsh punishment. It sits in the middle — firm and serious, but still relatively gentle:

```
Gentle hint → Admonition → Reprimand → Punishment
```

  • A gentle hint is soft and easy to ignore: "Maybe you should study a bit more."
  • An admonition is firmer and carries weight: "I'm warning you — if you keep neglecting your studies, you will regret it."
  • A reprimand is sharper and more critical, often after a mistake has already been made.
  • A punishment is an actual consequence — action taken against someone.

An admonition lives in that second slot. It's weighted with seriousness, but its spirit is guidance, not attack.
Who Gives Admonitions, and To Whom?

Admonitions almost always flow from someone with authority, wisdom, or deep concern toward someone who needs guidance. For example:

  • A parent warning a child not to keep lying, because it will damage their character.
  • A teacher cautioning students against academic dishonesty before an exam.
  • A judge formally warning a lawyer or defendant in a courtroom to behave properly.
  • A religious leader urging their community to avoid greed or cruelty.
  • A mentor telling a young professional not to burn bridges in their career.
  • A friend earnestly telling another friend that their drinking is getting out of hand.

In each case, the person giving the admonition cares about what happens next. The admonition is meant to steer, not to destroy.

In everyday life, an admonition can be a spoken warning between any two people — informal, personal, and direct.

In formal contexts (legal, religious, institutional), an admonition can be an official, recorded warning — for example, a judge issuing an admonition to a witness to tell the truth, or a church formally cautioning a member about their conduct.

The word itself leans slightly formal in tone, so you'll encounter it more in writing, speeches, literature, and serious conversations than in everyday casual chat.

To sharpen your understanding, here are the defining characteristics:

It is verbal or written. An admonition is always expressed in words — spoken or written. A disapproving look is not an admonition.

It is serious in tone. It is never trivial. The person giving it means business.

It is corrective in purpose. It aims to fix behavior, prevent a mistake, or guide someone toward the right path.

It is not a punishment. An admonition is a warning, not a consequence. It's what comes before things go wrong, or right at the edge of things going wrong.

It often implies authority or care. The person giving it usually has a reason to be concerned — either because of their position or because they genuinely care about the person receiving it.

• The coach's admonition to "never give up, no matter the score" stayed with him for the rest of his life.
  • She ignored her doctor's admonition to rest, and her condition worsened.
  • The judge issued a stern admonition to the jury not to discuss the case with anyone outside the courtroom.
  • His grandmother's admonitions about honesty shaped who he became as a man.
  • Despite repeated admonitions from her manager, she continued arriving late to meetings.
An admonition is a serious, earnest warning or cautionary piece of advice — firm in tone, caring in intent — meant to correct someone's behavior or prevent them from making a harmful mistake.

Think of it this way: if someone gives you an admonition, they are saying — "I am warning you, seriously, because I want things to go well for you." It's the voice of wisdom stepping in before damage is done.
355:
Something admonitory is anything that carries a warning, a caution, or a gentle rebuke — it signals to someone that they are doing something wrong, or that they need to be more careful, or that they should stop a certain behavior.

Think of it this way: when a parent gives their child that look across the dinner table — the one that says "don't you dare do that again" — that look is admonitory. It isn't a punishment. It isn't a compliment. It's a warning dressed up in a glance.

Admonitory sits in a very specific emotional space. It is:

  • Firmer than friendly advice — it's not just a casual suggestion
  • Softer than a threat or condemnation — it doesn't punish, it warns
  • Often tinged with authority — it usually comes from someone in a position to correct you: a parent, a teacher, a boss, a mentor, an elder
  • Sometimes mixed with care — the person warning you often does so because they want you to do better, not simply to scold you

So the word carries a sense of corrective seriousness — the attitude of someone who sees a problem and wants it addressed before it gets worse.

The word is used to describe things like:

  • A tone of voice — "She spoke in an admonitory tone when she reminded him of the rules."
  • A look or gesture — "His admonitory glance silenced the room."
  • A letter or note — "The manager sent an admonitory email to the team after the missed deadline."
  • Words or remarks — "She ended her speech with a few admonitory words about the dangers of overconfidence."
  • A finger wag, a raised eyebrow, a pause — any signal that means watch yourself.

Essentially, any act, expression, or communication that is meant to warn, caution, or mildly reprimand someone can be called admonitory.

1. The teacher gave the chatty students an admonitory look, and they immediately went quiet.
  2. His grandmother placed an admonitory hand on his shoulder and told him to choose his words wisely.
  3. The report ended with an admonitory note, warning that future violations would not be tolerated.
  4. She raised an admonitory finger before he could even finish his sentence.
  5. The coach's tone became admonitory when he noticed his players were not taking warm-ups seriously.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what admonitory is clearly different from:

  • Threatening — A threat says "I will punish you." Admonitory says "You should correct yourself." One promises consequences; the other urges change.
  • Praising / Encouraging — The opposite end of the spectrum. Admonitory is corrective, not affirming.
  • Condemning / Accusatory — Condemnation judges you harshly for what you've already done. Admonitory is more forward-looking — it points to what you should do differently going ahead.
  • Instructive (in a neutral sense) — A science textbook is instructive. An admonitory message has a moral or behavioral charge to it — it's not just teaching facts, it's correcting conduct.
The Underlying Logic of the Word

If you break down what the word does conceptually: it describes the quality of serving as a warning or a rebuke. When you say something has an admonitory quality, you are saying it functions like a firm, authoritative nudge — a signal from one person to another that says: this behavior is not acceptable, or this path is dangerous, and you would do well to change course.

It is the adjective form of the act of admonishing — which means to warn someone seriously, or to urge them to correct their behavior, usually from a place of some authority or concern.

Admonitory = warning-like, cautionary, mildly rebuking in nature.

Whenever something — a tone, a look, a word, a gesture, a letter — is designed or felt to say "be careful," "stop that," or "you need to do better," that thing is admonitory.

Ado means unnecessary fuss, commotion, or trouble surrounding something — especially when that fuss seems bigger than it needs to be.

Think of a situation where people are making a lot of noise, rushing around, arguing, or getting worked up over something that is actually simple or not worth all that energy. That excessive reaction — all that drama and bother — is the ado.

The word carries a built-in sense of disproportionateness. When you use "ado," you are subtly suggesting that the fuss is overdone, unwarranted, or could easily be skipped.

Imagine your family is trying to leave the house for a short trip. One person can't find their keys. Another is arguing about which route to take. Someone else is complaining that no one is ready. There's noise, stress, and chaos — all before the trip has even started.

All of that commotion? That's ado. The trip itself is simple, but getting there involves a whole lot of fuss and bother.
How It Behaves in a Sentence

"Ado" is an uncountable noun. This means:

  • ✅ There was much ado.
  • ✅ After all the ado, nothing changed.
  • ❌ There was an ado. (wrong — you wouldn't say this)
  • ❌ There were many ados. (wrong — it has no plural form)

You treat it like words such as chaos, noise, or fuss — things you can have more or less of, but not count individually.
The Phrases Where You Will Meet "Ado" Most Often

This word lives almost entirely inside a small number of fixed phrases. Learning these phrases is essential, because "ado" on its own (outside of them) is quite rare and old-fashioned in everyday speech.

1. "Without further ado"
